planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed; Dale is a mid-season syrup sorghum developed at the US Sugar Crops Field Station in Meridian, Mississippi, and its reliable standing ability and disease tolerance have made it a workhorse variety for Gulf South cane patches.

directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once the danger of frost has passed, thinning stands to their final spacing to encourage thick, juice-heavy stalks. Dale grows upright on medium stalks covered with a waxy bloom and stands well through late-season winds, resisting anthracnose, red rot, and maize dwarf mosaic better than many older Southern syrup cultivars. Cut canes for pressing once seed heads reach the hard-dough stage, then mill and boil the juice promptly, since the mild, amber, good-bodied syrup Dale is prized for depends on getting cut stalks to the evaporator before their sugar content drops. Leftover bagasse and grain heads can be fed to livestock or left standing for birds after the cane harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed well past last frost; M81E is a late-maturing, full-season syrup sorghum bred at Mississippi State's agricultural experiment station, so it needs the Gulf South's long, hot growing season to reach its towering 10-12 foot height and load its stalks with sugar.

directions: Sow seed roughly an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has thoroughly warmed, thinning to final spacing as seedlings establish. M81E is a tall, late-season Mississippi-bred syrup cultivar with brown seed heads that needs a longer stretch of hot weather than earlier varieties like Dale to fully mature, making it especially well suited to the long warm season along the Gulf Coast. Harvest when the canes reach hard-dough stage in the seed head and the lower leaves begin to dry, then press and boil the juice quickly into a mild, light amber syrup. Because of its late maturity, gardeners in shorter-season areas should get it in the ground as early as safely possible after frost to ensure the stalks finish sweetening before fall's first cold snap.
sources: MAFES Foundation Seed Stocks — 'M-81E: A New Variety of Sweet Sorghum'
National Sweet Sorghum Producers and Processors Association

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil well after last frost; Theis is a tall, late-maturing Mid-South syrup sorghum that ripens two to three weeks behind mid-season varieties like Dale, so it rewards gardeners with a long, hot growing season such as the Gulf Coast provides.

directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has fully passed, thinning seedlings to allow thick, sturdy canes to develop. Theis is a Mid-South heirloom syrup sorghum distributed through Mississippi's foundation seed program, growing noticeably taller and maturing later than standard varieties like Dale, and it holds up well to some of the organophosphate insecticides sometimes used on nearby cotton fields. Let the canes stand until the seed heads reach hard-dough stage before cutting and pressing, since Theis is valued for producing a notably mild, high-quality syrup once the juice is boiled down. Because of its long season, it performs best where summers run hot and frost-free well into fall.

common_name: Honey Drip Sorghum (Southern Heirloom Syrup Sorghum)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil well after the last frost; Honey Drip is a regionally acclimated Southern heirloom syrup sorghum valued for its drought and heat tolerance, reliable yields, and comparatively early maturity for a syrup type.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in average, well-drained garden soil once the ground has warmed after frost, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Honey Drip is a Southern heirloom syrup sorghum that has been grown and re-selected in the region for generations, giving it strong heat and drought tolerance and dependable yields on soils too lean or dry for some other syrup canes. Plants top out shorter than many syrup sorghums, with upright, honey-colored seed heads, and reach cutting stage somewhat earlier in the season than late-maturing types. Harvest canes at hard-dough stage and press promptly, since the sweet, mellow syrup Honey Drip is known for depends on getting the juice to the evaporator soon after cutting.
